nameStory: The anhinga gets its nickname 'snakebird' from its eerie swimming behavior - only its long, slender neck appears above water, looking exactly like a snake ready to strike! The name 'anhinga' comes from the Brazilian Tupi word 'a'ñinga,' meaning 'devil bird' or 'snake bird.' Early observers were so struck by this serpentine appearance that the bird earned multiple snake-related names across different cultures.
description: The anhinga is a sleek, dark waterbird that looks like a cross between a cormorant and a heron. These skilled underwater hunters have long, pointed bills perfect for spearing fish, and necks that can strike with lightning speed. Males are glossy black with silver-white streaks on their wings, while females have buff-colored heads and necks. They're large birds, about the size of a great blue heron, with a distinctive long tail and narrow wings.

idTips.label: Snake-like swimming
idTips.description: When swimming, only the long, S-curved neck appears above water, moving with a sinuous motion that looks exactly like a swimming snake

idTips.label: Dagger-sharp bill
idTips.description: The bill is long, straight, and needle-sharp - noticeably more pointed than a cormorant's hooked bill, designed for spearing rather than grasping fish

idTips.label: Spread-wing drying pose
idTips.description: Often perches with wings spread wide open to dry, holding this cruciform position motionlessly for long periods in sunny spots

idTips.label: Glossy black plumage
idTips.description: Males have deep black feathers with an almost metallic sheen, while females show warm brown and buff coloring on the head and neck

idTips.label: Long, fan-shaped tail
idTips.description: The tail is noticeably longer and more prominent than a cormorant's, often held spread like a fan when perched or swimming

habitat: In New England, anhingas are extremely rare visitors found only occasionally along southern coastal areas, particularly in Rhode Island and southern Massachusetts. They prefer warm, sheltered freshwater ponds, slow-moving rivers, and brackish marshes with abundant fish and plenty of sunny perches for drying their wings. Look for them near cypress swamps, wooded ponds, or quiet coves where they can hunt undisturbed.

seasonality.spring: Very rare spring visitors may appear in late April or May, often after strong southern weather systems push them northward from their usual range.
seasonality.summer: Most New England sightings occur during summer months when these heat-loving birds are most likely to wander north during particularly warm periods.
seasonality.fall: Occasional fall migrants pass through in September, though still extremely uncommon and usually involving single birds rather than flocks.
seasonality.winter: Essentially absent from New England in winter, as they require warm temperatures and unfrozen water for their fishing lifestyle.

funFact: Anhingas have no external nostrils and breathe entirely through their throat opening, which allows them to dive underwater with their sharp bills without water rushing into their respiratory system - like having a built-in snorkel system in reverse!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with cormorants, but anhingas have much sharper, pointed bills (not hooked), longer tails, and that distinctive snake-like neck posture when swimming. Remember: if it looks like a swimming snake, it's probably an anhinga - cormorants keep more of their body visible when swimming.
contextualKnowledge: The anhinga is sometimes called 'water turkey' due to its habit of spreading its tail feathers like a turkey's fan, though it's completely unrelated to turkeys. These birds are primarily southern species, making any New England sighting a noteworthy event worth reporting to local birding communities.
compareHints: Anhingas are the only members of the darter family in the Americas, so confusion typically involves cormorants from the closely related family Phalacrocoracidae. Unlike cormorants, anhingas have straight spear-like bills rather than hooked ones, swim with only their necks visible, and have much more prominent tails. Their hunting style is also different - anhingas actively spear fish underwater while cormorants grab prey with their bills.
